description: FitRAG evaluation set. Categories: in_scope (answerable from KB), ambiguous (under-specified but partially answerable), out_of_scope (refuse). expected_sources lists PDF file stems that should appear in a correct retrieval.

questions.question: How many days per week of muscle-strengthening activity does the WHO recommend for adults?
questions.reference_answer: At least 2 days per week of muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups.

questions.question: What weekly aerobic activity minimum does the WHO recommend for adults?
questions.reference_answer: 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity, or 75-150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week (or an equivalent combination).

questions.question: What is progressive overload?
questions.reference_answer: The gradual increase of stress placed on the body during training (load, volume, frequency, intensity, complexity) so that adaptation continues and progress does not plateau.

questions.question: How many sets and reps should a beginner perform per exercise according to NSCA guidance for older adults / novices?
questions.reference_answer: About 2-3 sets per exercise, 10-15 repetitions at a lower relative resistance for beginners.

questions.question: According to Starting Strength's 'Who Wants to Be a Novice?', how often should a novice train per week and with what rest pattern?
questions.reference_answer: Three sessions per week, training then resting roughly 48 hours, with a longer (~72 hour) rest after the third session of the week.

questions.question: Is resistance training safe for children and adolescents according to the NSCA youth position statement?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. A properly designed and supervised resistance training program is safe and effective for children and adolescents and can offer health, fitness, and performance benefits.

questions.question: What are the main benefits of resistance training for older adults?
questions.reference_answer: Improvements in muscle strength, power, muscle mass, physical function, mobility, bone health, and reductions in fall risk and chronic disease impact.

questions.question: What is long-term athletic development (LTAD)?
questions.reference_answer: A multi-stage, long-term approach to nurturing physical and psychosocial development across childhood and adolescence to support lifelong physical activity and athletic performance.

questions.question: What does the NSCA recommend regarding qualified instruction and supervision for youth resistance training?
questions.reference_answer: Youth resistance training should be conducted with qualified instruction and supervision, in a safe environment, with a dynamic warm-up and a focus on proper technique.

questions.question: What variables can be manipulated to create progressive overload?
questions.reference_answer: Variables include load/resistance, repetitions, sets, frequency, training density, speed/velocity, range of motion, and exercise complexity.

questions.question: Does the WHO recommend any physical activity even for people who cannot meet the full guidelines?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. Doing some physical activity is better than doing none; people who cannot meet the recommendations should still be as active as their abilities allow.

questions.question: What does NSCA say about weightlifting (Olympic-style lifts) for sports performance?
questions.reference_answer: Weightlifting exercises and their derivatives are an effective method to develop muscular power and improve sports performance when properly programmed and supervised.

questions.question: What is the recommended frequency of resistance training per muscle group for older adults?
questions.reference_answer: 2-3 days per week per muscle group, performed on non-consecutive days.

questions.question: How does continuous running combined with strength endurance training affect muscular endurance according to the JUMORA study?
questions.reference_answer: The combination of strength endurance training with continuous running improves muscular endurance compared to baseline.

questions.question: What does the progressive overload scoping review say about how progressive overload is reported in long-term exercise studies?
questions.reference_answer: Reporting of progressive overload parameters is inconsistent in the literature; few studies examine progressive overload as an independent variable, limiting strong conclusions.

questions.question: What warm-up does the NSCA recommend before a youth resistance training session?
questions.reference_answer: A 5- to 10-minute dynamic warm-up at the start of each training session.

questions.question: Why does Rippetoe argue that a novice should do only a few basic barbell exercises rather than many machine exercises?
questions.reference_answer: Because basic compound barbell lifts drive the most growth and strength gains for a novice; only a handful of exercises are needed for several months, and extras can interfere with recovery.

questions.question: What does the WHO say about sedentary behaviour for adults?
questions.reference_answer: Adults should limit the amount of time spent being sedentary and replace sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity for health benefits.

questions.question: How should training load progress for a true novice according to Starting Strength?
questions.reference_answer: Start with light weights (even an empty bar), perform sets of 5, and add small increments each workout while form remains good.

questions.question: What recovery considerations does the NSCA LTAD position statement emphasize?
questions.reference_answer: Rest and recovery should be scheduled as mandatory parts of the training plan to optimise physical development and minimise accumulated fatigue, regardless of coach or parental pressure.

questions.question: How much should I train?
questions.reference_answer: Depends on goals and population, but the WHO baseline is 150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous aerobic activity per week plus muscle-strengthening 2+ days/week; novice strength programs typically run 2-3 sessions/week.

questions.question: Is more training always better?
questions.reference_answer: No. Rest and recovery are mandatory; excessive training without recovery accumulates fatigue and harms adaptation.

questions.question: What is the best workout?
questions.reference_answer: There is no single 'best' workout in the sources; the right program depends on age, goals, and experience. The KB only provides general guidelines (frequency, intensity, progression).

questions.question: Should children lift weights?
questions.reference_answer: Yes, when properly supervised and programmed: NSCA endorses youth resistance training for safety, health and performance benefits.

questions.question: How do older adults stay strong?
questions.reference_answer: Through regular resistance training 2-3 days/week per muscle group at appropriate intensity, with progressive overload, supporting muscle, bone, and functional health.
